source.title: When Does Preconditioning Help or Hurt Generalization?
source.authors: S. Amari; Jimmy Ba; R. Grosse; Xuechen Li; Atsushi Nitanda; Taiji Suzuki; Denny Wu; Ji Xu

record.tranche_reason: The study reports epoch-wise non-monotonicity and multiple peaks in generalization-risk components, refining the scope and possible form of double descent.
record.gate_note: The study explicitly examines epoch-wise non-monotonicity in Appendix A.2 and multiple-descent behavior over the overparameterization ratio in Appendix C.1. Its optimizer, noise, misspecification, and interpolation experiments do not otherwise test the claim's size-wise or sample-size-wise double-descent versions. Cited findings from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: A preconditioning paper whose appendices report double-descent-type results in anisotropic ridgeless linear regression. GD's bias is non-monotone over time near the threshold, which the authors call epoch-wise double descent (A.2, Fig 12). Bias and variance show multiple peaks over γ>1 (C.1, Fig 15). The authors argue this epoch-wise mechanism (bias, not variance) may differ from the deep-network one, which bears on the form of V2, V4 and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record overstates the double-descent content. The paper's main conclusion concerns preconditioning: GD vs NGD generalization depends on label noise, misspecification and signal alignment. NGD is better under noise, misspecification or misalignment; GD is better otherwise. Interpolating between GD and NGD, or early stopping, manages the bias-variance tradeoff, and preconditioning speeds risk decay in RKHS. Double-descent-type curves are side remarks in the appendices. The authors caution that their epoch-wise mechanism, which lives in the bias term, may not explain the deep-network findings, where the variance is thought to be non-monotone.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes optimizer-dependent population risk in linear and kernel regression and runs optimizer comparisons in neural networks; it does not reproduce the original model-size or sample-size sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported non-monotonicity depends on the signal covariance and feature spectrum; epoch-wise non-monotonicity is reported for GD but not NGD in the stated setup.
record.problems: The claim-related epoch-wise and multiple-descent evidence is limited to linear-regression risk components and specific covariance settings. The multiple-descent figures provide qualitative curves rather than uncertainty estimates; the text does not establish the corresponding behavior in deep networks.
record.rows_left_out: Neural-network label-noise, misspecification, and optimizer-interpolation results in Sections 5 and Appendix C.3 compare optimizer generalization but do not measure a double-descent curve over model size, epochs, or sample count. No separately reported claim-related outcomes were otherwise omitted.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep in deep networks.
No epoch-wise test-error curve in deep networks, and no total-risk curve with label noise.
Whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peaks.

missing.what: Proposition 6: variance increases monotonically with time for all preconditioners, so variance cannot produce epoch-wise non-monotonicity in this model.
With isotropic prior Σθ=I, GD expected bias decreases monotonically over time, so there is no epoch-wise double descent.
missing.locator: Appendix A.2; Appendix D.8 eq. D.23

missing.what: With ΣX=I, bias and variance are monotone for γ>1 (stated as known, citing HMRT19), in contrast with Fig 15.
Variance lower bound σ²/(γ-1), attained by NGD: it diverges near γ→1 and decreases with γ, a second-descent shape for variance.

record.verdict_notes: All claim-relevant results are qualitative figures in linear regression; the neural-network experiments in Section 5 do not measure double-descent curves. The tranche could arguably be T3, but the explicit argument that the bias rather than the variance drives epoch-wise non-monotonicity makes T5 reasonable.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep in deep networks testing a fall-rise-fall test-error curve near the just-fit threshold.
The reported epoch-wise result is for a linear-regression bias/generalization-risk component, not a deep-network test-error sweep; the variance contribution to an epoch-wise curve is not tested.
No training-sample-size sweep near the interpolation threshold.
The reported risk-component curves are for overparameterized linear regression under a particular anisotropic setup; the study does not establish the general curve across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting the peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.
The study reports multiple peaks in linear-regression risk components, but does not test whether label noise drives those peaks or whether optimally tuned regularization removes them.
No re-counting of complexity by an effective number of parameters is tested.
